Being emotionally close or intimate with others

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette:
Daniel, a 32-year-old European American man who worked as a tutor, came to treatment after months of living as though ordinary life might again turn into something unmanageable. Before the stalking began, he had described himself as steady and private, someone who spent most of his days helping students prepare for exams and moving between tutoring appointments and home with his wife. The stalking started with small intrusions that at first seemed easy to dismiss: repeated appearances by the same man near places Daniel frequented, messages that implied he was being watched, and a sense that his routines were no longer his own. Over time the pattern became impossible to ignore. Daniel found himself scanning parking lots before getting out of the car, checking windows and doorways, and wondering whether the figure he had glimpsed earlier in the day was still nearby. What had once felt like coincidence came to feel deliberate, and he began to live with the constant impression that he was being followed or tracked.

The period after the stalking ended in the practical sense did not bring relief in the way Daniel had expected. Instead, he noticed that his attention kept catching on signs of potential threat, even in places where nothing was actually happening. A motorcycle passing close by could jolt him hard enough that he would stop speaking mid-sentence and look up sharply, as if bracing for the next approach. He reacted the same way when someone's voice rose, even if the anger was not directed at him and even if the person sounded calm rather than explosive; the tone alone could make him tense and watchful, as though anger in another person might signal danger. He came to trust unfamiliar places less and less, especially if he could not immediately assess exits, sightlines, or who might be there. This meant he started declining new tutoring assignments in settings he did not know well, choosing instead to work only in locations that felt predictable, which slowly narrowed his professional flexibility.

At home, Daniel's wife noticed that he rarely seemed settled. He had trouble falling asleep and, when he did sleep, he would wake repeatedly, listening for sounds outside the bedroom or replaying the day's movements in his mind. He began to avoid relaxing altogether because stillness felt unsafe to him; sitting with a book, lying on the sofa, or letting himself drift into a quiet evening brought on a feeling that he was exposing himself to danger. Even in moments that should have been restful, he stayed keyed up, as if his body had not received the message that the immediate threat was over. He often described these reactions with embarrassment, saying that he knew nothing was actually wrong in those moments but that his body behaved as if he were still in the middle of being hunted.

Daniel's thoughts about the experience grew harsher as the months went on. He told himself that he deserved to suffer because of what had happened, and there was a bleak, self-punishing tone to the way he talked about coping. He doubted that he would do the right thing if confronted with a difficult situation again, and that uncertainty made him increasingly cautious in ways that spilled into everyday life. He became less willing to trust people's intentions, saying that people were not what they seemed and that people could not be trusted. This mistrust extended beyond strangers to social situations more generally, and he found himself watching people for inconsistencies, scanning for signs that they might be hiding something. Emotional closeness also became harder to tolerate. With his wife, he remained loving in practical ways, but he pulled back from intimacy and avoided the kind of open emotional contact that used to feel natural. He seemed to worry that letting himself be close would make him vulnerable again, though he did not frame it as fear so much as a grim decision to keep a safer distance.

By the time he sought help, Daniel's days had become smaller and more managed around these concerns. He would take familiar routes, avoid unfamiliar streets, and plan his tutoring schedule around places he knew well. He had begun to notice the cost of this pattern in his work and in the strain it placed on his marriage, yet he also felt he could not simply relax or trust his own judgment enough to do otherwise. What finally brought him to treatment was the growing sense that he was living on constant alert and could no longer tell whether he was protecting himself or disappearing into fear. He arrived hoping for some way to feel safe again without having to keep shrinking his life, though what frightened him most was the possibility that he would never fully trust other people, or himself, enough to let his guard down.
